name: Nancowry
confidence_why: Radhakrishnan 1981 and Rajasingh 2014 and 2016, two independent fieldworkers, both put word stress on the lexical root with affixes unstressed, differing only on whether suffixes are occasionally stressed and on whether disyllabic roots exist.
catalog_citation: Radhakrishnan, R. 1981. The Nancowry Word: Phonology, Affixal Morphology and Roots of a Nicobarese Language. (Current Inquiry into Language and Linguistics 37.) Edmonton: Linguistic Research Inc. Read via archive.org item micro_IA41153606_0076 (scanned full text).
catalog_quote: 1.2 Placement of stress. The Nancowry words are analyzable into roots and affixes, and the stress occurs always on the root and is not phonetically predictable. Roots are never more than two syllables in length. If the root is disyllabic the stress falls on the second syllable. In this fashion it is seen that, given morphological information, a single rule will place the stress correctly on a form. But, roots may occur with a varying number of intervening affixed syllables. Also, when the vocalic in the stressed syllable is complex (V1V2), only one of the vocalics get stressed, and it could be either V1 or V2. Therefore, the incidence of stress must somehow be marked in the surface representation. However, it could be assigned as shown above by a rule at the underlying level where root identity could be marked.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Nancowry with an empty rule. This work supplies the rule: root stress (morphologically determined), second syllable of a disyllabic root. Nothing in the catalog contradicts it.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress always falls on the root, never on an affix; roots are at most two syllables, and in a disyllabic root the stress falls on the second syllable. Placement is not phonetically predictable (affixes of varying number may precede or follow the root) but is fully predictable given morphological information. Stressed vowels are lengthened (fully in open syllables, half in closed), and vowel nasality is contrastive but occurs only on stressed root vowels. In a diphthong only one of the two vowels bears the stress and it may be either one, which is why stress must be marked in surface representation.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. Two-root compounds are listed among the examples (e.g. [kuysini.en] 'hip', [ku.enkapow] 'cow', described as 'two roots'), with stressed syllables underscored in the original, but the underscoring is lost in the scanned text layer, so whether each root keeps a stress cannot be verified from the file.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions; English borrowings [tarap] 'to trap', [kilas] 'glass tumbler' are treated as disyllabic roots and stressed by the same rule. p. 28: 'Stress in general lengthens the duration of the vocalic'; full length in open syllables, less than half-length in closed; nasality does not occur on unstressed vowels (p. 28).
new_statements.identity_note: Rajasingh 2014 and 2016 describe 'Muot', which he identifies as the language 'known as Nancowry or Central Nicobarese' spoken on Nancowry, Katchal and Kamorta islands (2016 p. 14; 2014 p. 104), with data collected on Nancowry Island; same variety as Radhakrishnan 1981's Nancowry. The listed 1976 note is also on Nancowry.

new_statements.quote: The sound system of the language is sufficiently characterized by reference to the phonemes/segments and syllables; there is no contrastive tone or phonation, and stress – although important – is generally fixed on lexical roots. (p. 24) [...] The syllables are found stressed or unstressed, and when stressed they are phonetically tensed and lengthened. This extends to full length in the case of open syllables and to half long in the case of closed syllables. The syllables are found stressed invariably when they happen to be the lexical root and occasionally when happen to be of suffixal ones (compare, for example, the unstressed form of the suffix jən in the word muklɑˑklɑjən 'defender' with its stressed form jəˑn in the word cumjɑːʔijəˑn 'to free'). (p. 25)

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with Radhakrishnan 1981 on root stress and on the stress-length correlation; adds the observation that suffixes are occasionally stressed and that there is no contrastive tone or phonation. Catalog rule is empty, so this fills it rather than contradicts it.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No contrastive tone or phonation; stress is generally fixed on the lexical root (all roots monosyllabic in this analysis). Stressed syllables are tensed and lengthened (full length in open syllables, half-long in closed). Suffix syllables are occasionally stressed too (e.g. jəˑn in cumjɑːʔijəˑn 'to free' vs unstressed jən in muklɑˑklɑjən 'defender'). Within a diphthong either the first or the second vowel target carries the stress/length, apparently predictably by utterance position (koˑən in isolation / utterance-finally vs koəˑn elsewhere).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; the occasional stress on suffix syllables (p. 25) is the closest thing to a second stress in a word.
new_statements.exceptions: Suffixes occasionally stressed (p. 25; p. 22 fn. 12: 'The sketch grammar presented here finds non-root syllables also as occasionally stressed and tensed'). p. 22 fn. 13: this analysis recognizes all roots as monosyllabic, unlike Radhakrishnan's disyllabic roots.

The listed 1976 note is also on Nancowry.

new_statements.relation_note: Same root-stress placement as Radhakrishnan 1981 and Rajasingh 2016; adds the explicit non-phonemic statement. Fills the empty catalog rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is perceived but not phonemic; vowels are stressed and tensed invariably when they are the nucleus of a root syllable, and unstressed/lax in affixal syllables (e.g. root ciˑn 'what' vs affixes -si-, -se in juɑˑŋsise 'progressive'). Tensing goes to full length in open and half length in closed syllables; in diphthongs the stress/tenseness sits on either the initial or the final vowel.
new_statements.exceptions: None beyond the diphthong detail: 'the stress and the tenseness are found to occur either with the initial vowel sounds.. or with the final ones' (p. 106).

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on placement: all three opened sources put word stress on the lexical root, with affixes unstressed. Two points differ in detail. (1) Radhakrishnan 1981 (p. 15) recognizes disyllabic roots and puts the stress on their second syllable, while Rajasingh 2016 (p. 22 fn. 13) treats all roots as monosyllabic, so for him the second-syllable clause does not arise; the surface facts are the same, the morphological analysis differs. (2) Radhakrishnan says stress falls 'always on the root'; Rajasingh 2016 (p. 25; p. 22 fn. 12) finds suffix syllables 'occasionally' stressed and tensed. Radhakrishnan's 'not phonetically predictable' (p. 15) and Rajasingh 2014's 'not found to be phonemic' (p. 105 fn. 6) are compatible: stress is predictable from morphology (root identity), hence non-contrastive, but not from the phonological string alone.
